sources.title: Tigranakert archaeological expedition, Tigranakert in written sources
sources.note: Direct expedition account read; use the paragraph connecting the twelfth- and thirteenth-century Khachen landscape with the excavated medieval settlement. Polemical modern territorial commentary and unqualified ancient identification claims are not adopted. Geometry comes from independent local atlas decoding.

sources.title: Research on Armenian Architecture, Dadivank khachkar of 1182: Armenian transcription and English translation
sources.note: Direct Armenian transcription read; English counterpart https://www.armenianarchitecture.org/public/en/monuments/2637 also read. Sample ԵՍ ՀԱՍԱՆ is exactly the opening two words after the date, modern type of a medieval inscription. All uses grouped with prior runtime RAA Dadivank hall 2592 because both derive from Karapetian 2001 / Corpus of Armenian Epigraphy 5. English translation mistranslates the forty-year phrase; public text omits that detail and uses only secure family/transfer clauses.

sources.title: Tigranakert archaeological expedition, Early Christian square: medieval residential layers
sources.note: Direct stratigraphic account read. Eleventh to mid-twelfth-century layer: clay floors, pits, tonirs up to 1.5 metres; late twelfth to early thirteenth-century layer: semi-underground complex, narrow passages, reed roofs on wooden columns. Ildegizid coin chronology and church destruction cause not used.

sources.title: Tigranakert archaeological expedition, The Medieval Tools and Weapons
sources.note: Direct full text read. Figure 4 chopping knife and figure 9 mill runner both eleventh to twelfth century; medieval worn whetstones. Avoid conflicting ploughshare captions and much earlier spear/later sword.

sources.title: Tigranakert archaeological expedition, Medieval pottery and glass
sources.note: Direct artifact descriptions and figure captions read. Grain jar on twelfth-century floor; bird/vegetal glazed plates twelfth to thirteenth century; glass bracelets broadly ninth to thirteenth. No object automatically treated as exact year 1100.

sources.title: Tigranakert archaeological expedition, The Canal
sources.note: Direct technical report read: 2006/2020 investigations, 300-metre excavated rock-cut stretch, open sections and tunnels, limestone floor intended to reduce water loss. Continuous use until mid-thirteenth century is explicitly the excavation team’s interpretation. No sewer, toilet or potability claim.

sources.title: Tamar Minasyan, The writing centers and manuscript heritage of Artsakh (AIEA)
sources.note: Direct article by Matenadaran senior researcher read. Mkhitar Gosh 1184 manuscript for Vakhtang and Arzukhatun; 1204 Haterk/Khadavank library inscription. Autograph status not asserted, because another scholarly account calls it probable. Later manuscripts not projected into twelfth century.

sources.title: Robert W. Thomson, The Lawcode (Datastanagirk’) of Mxit’ar Goš (Rodopi, 2000), publisher description
sources.note: Original publisher description in Google Books directly indexed: began 1184, secular and ecclesiastical matters, subsequent influence in Cilicia and diaspora. No claims of complete enforcement or detailed statutes inferred from summary.

sources.title: Mkhitar Gosh, Fables, translated by Robert Bedrosian: 168 and 173, with translator’s introduction
sources.note: Direct translation and https://www.attalus.org/armenian/goshint.htm read. All pages of this work grouped. Introduction dates author to late twelfth/early thirteenth century and places him with Vakhtang’s household in Khachen; no assertion each fable was composed there or before 1200. Fables 168/173 are literary evidence, not literal events or medical instructions.

sources.title: Claude Mutafian, Hasan Jalal, a great Armenian prince under the Mongols (AIEA)
sources.note: Direct scholarly article read. Later continuity only: Hasan Jalal from 1214, Gandzasar church 1216 to 1238/consecration 1240, Mongol accommodation, death 1260/61, descendants. Do not confuse this Hasan Jalal with Hasan son of Vakhtang in 1182. Modern political sovereignty is not inferred from medieval titles.

batchIdentityNotes.scope: Historical regional/princely landscape, not one verified kingdom frontier and not the modern Republic of Artsakh. No shared-card associations.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Single world-1100 polygon; bounds 45.863 to 47.817 E / 38.931 to 40.451 N. Rounded point checks include Tigranakert, Handaberd and Amaras, exclude Dadivank and Gandzasar. Public mismatch warning and excluded site locations repeated where relevant.
batchIdentityNotes.sourceLimits: Armenian institutional and excavation sources are used for specific material evidence and transcriptions, not their contemporary political rhetoric. The 1182 Hasan and later Hasan Jalal remain distinct. RAA English forty-year phrase has an apparent translation error, so it is omitted. Archaeological periods spanning 1200 are explicit; no exact year tags manufactured.
batchIdentityNotes.continuity: No modern sovereignty claim is made from medieval names, language or monuments. Armenia and Arran map records remain separate. End status continuity refers to communities and institutions, not unbroken state sovereignty.
